newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian state apologises for "stolen" children.
newsitem.headline: Australian state apologises for "stolen" children.

text.p: Australia's most populous state, New South Wales, offered an unreserved apology to Aborigines on Wednesday for policies which saw children "stolen" from their parents under forced assimilation schemes.
Premier Bob Carr moved the motion of apology in the state parliament, and acknowledged the roles of Australian authorities in the separation of Aboriginal children from their parents.
Carr told parliament a report by Australia's human rights watchdog detailing the harm of such policies, which continued into the late 1960s, should be responded to with compassion.

He invited Aboriginal groups to offer ideas for a permanent memorial to acknowledge the grief caused by forced assimilation and announced a A$100,000 (US$75,000) grant to a group which works to reunite Aboriginal families.

Prime Minister John Howard has rejected recommendations in the human rights authority's report that the national government make a formal apology and compensate the tens of thousands "stolen generation" Aborigines.
He instead offered a personal apology last month, saying he felt a deep sorrow for the past injustices.
About 1,500 Aborigines have begun legal claims for compensation and hundreds more are reported to be in the pipeline.

The New South Wales motion of apology, which was supported by the state's opposition leader and passed unanimously, followed an address to parliament by an Aboriginal woman who did not see her mother for 53 years after she was taken from her as a 14-month-old child.
Nancy de Vries said when the pair were finally reunited, her mother could not relate to her.
"For 53 years, she had been blotting out the fact that she had lost her child," she said.
De Vries told parliament she lived in 22 different houses before the age of 18.
"Growing up, I had to live with people who were always telling me that Aboriginal people were no good," she said.
Carr said later "no more moving and memorable words" had been heard in the state parliament in the past 150 years.
